doc.title: Ed Soph interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 9, 2024

title: Sitting in at fifteen and taking Dave Berry's gig
summary: His father makes him sit in on a Sunday session, Jimmy Ford approves, and Dave Berry hands him the gig.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: Were you sitting in, like there was a regular drummer there?
And they’d make some room for you?

Well what happened was the drummer who had the gig at this particular club that had Sunday afternoon sessions, was a fellow named Dave Berry, who unfortunately has left us, a very sweet man. Hell of a drummer. And it was Dave’s gig and he’d come over to my house a couple of times just to show me some things and then he’d have dinner, and we had a nice relationship. He came over on a break and said, “Eddie, do you want to sit in?” And man I was hoping the floor would open up and I could jump in the hole. Man I said, “No, no.” And my father leaned over and he said, “If you don’t get up and play those drums you’re never going to see your drums again.” So there was no room there for any negotiation. So I got up and I played, and it was really strange because I was so damn nervous I could hardly hold on to the sticks. But after playing the head of the tune and starting to get into the solos, all of a sudden I felt like I was at home playing with records only I didn’t know what was going to come out. But I knew how to play with a bass player because I’d been playing with Paul Chambers and Ray Brown and people like that on record.
You had the cream in your band there.

Yeah. So I got up to leave after the first tune and Jimmy Ford turned around and said, “Hey baby, no man, you sounds fine man, play another tune.” So I played another tune, I played the whole set. And then Dave came over after the gig and he said, “Eddie, the guys really like the way you play, I’m moving to Reno, Nevada in two weeks, would you like to take this gig?”

Yeah. So at the ripe old age of 15 I was playing with the “White Bird.” That’s what they called Jimmy Ford. Those recordings he made with Red Rodney at the Royal Roost, oh my God I’m going, I’m pinching myself.
Yeah you had the classic dream that most of us had at that age and it came true for you.
Yeah. Yeah. And once I got in the network then I started playing — I became a night person, it’s a wonder I made it through school because I was playing a lot of sessions © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-
